Bubble Boy

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Groundbreaking gene therapy offers hope for a rare immune condition.

Unique Selling Point:
A South African first and a globally leading gene therapy clinical trial. Ayaan Ahmed Sheik, a Cape Town child has received cutting edge and apparently successful gene therapy for the rare condition, Severe Combined Immunodeficiency. This is a story that speaks not only to fascinating new technology, but to the question of whether newborn screening should be implemented in SA hospitals.

Summary:
Ayaan Ahmed Sheik has spent almost all of his two years of life in hospital, battling a series of infections that threatened to end his short life. He was born with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, a rare condition that left him with no immune system at all - no defence against the hundreds of common infections that the rest of us brush off daily. Most children born with this condition die, because they are not diagnosed in time to rescue their embattled immune systems from common but - to them - life-threatening infections.

SCID children who are diagnosed early enough receive a bone marrow transplant - this must be carried out within their first three months of life for maximum effect. In Ayaan's case, there was a long delay in tissue typing and searching for a donor. When a potential donor was found, it was only a partial match and his mother Shamaa considered the risk to be too high.

In desperation, Shamaa reached out to St Jude Children's Hospital in Memphis Tennessee, where a clinical trial was testing ground-breaking new gene therapy for treatment of SCID. Ayaan was eventually accepted into the trial and after a long journey filled with stress and setbacks, he is now home in Cape Town, apparently able to start a normal life at last.

Further information:
1. SEVERE COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY
Severe Combined Immunodeficiency is the most severe of the genetic PIDs (primary immunodeficiencies) and essentially means that you have no functioning immune system. It was first made famous by "Bubble Boy" David Vetter (b 1971), who lived until the age of 12 in a sterile bubble, before he received a bone marrow transplant that unfortunately carried an Epstein-Barr virus and killed him shortly afterwards. The story attracted enormous press attention at the time, and inspired the movies The Boy in the Plastic Bubble (1976, starring John Travolta) and Bubble Boy (2001, starring Jake Gyllenhaal), as well as a musical.

Ayaan's SCID first manifested as severe and sudden illness within days of his birth. No one knew what was wrong until emergency exploratory surgery revealed multiple abscesses on his liver (an infection had entered through his umbilical cord). According to Shamaa, Ayaan is the only infant survivor of multiple liver abscesses. Following the surgery, Ayaan continued to present with severe infections and was eventually diagnosed with SCID. It’s usually an x-linked condition that is inherited from your mother, but in Ayaan’s case it is a spontaneous mutation.

2. ST JUDE CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL
Initially Ayaan was too old for the St Jude clinical trial but while Shamaa was in contact with them, they amended their protocol and accepted Ayaan into their programme. St Jude is a no-fee hospital funded entirely by celebrity donors. This particular trial, which is called LVXSCID-ND, covers 12 children for 5 years at a total cost of $28 million ($2.3 million per child). The hospital funds everything for them - housing, social worker, interpreters. After the children complete initial treatment, they are followed and supported by St Jude until they reach adulthood.

3. GENE THERAPY
Gene therapy has been considered for many years as a way to cure certain types of PID. But there was one very high profile clinical trial in which several of the subjects developed leukaemia following the therapy, and it got a bad name (the vector was inserted next to an important leukaemia inhibitor). The doctors at St Jude have developed a new vector which uses the HIV virus to transport the corrected genes through the body’s cells.

4. AYAAN'S TREATMENT
Ayaan's treatment went well, but there were complications caused by the fact that he, like all other SA-born babies, received a mandatory live BCG vaccine days after his birth. This caused a TB-type infection on his bones. His parents both accompanied him to the States, where they had to juggle treatment and care of their son during the day, with attempting to maintain their jobs at a distance by night. His mother returned home due to ill-health and stress late in 2017, and Ayaan and his dad finally came home in January 2018. They are now adjusting to life in SA, including introducing Ayaan to family members who have never seen him. Shamaa's teenage daughter from a previous marriage was left behind while Ayaan received his treatment and the family is now reintegrating.

5. NEWBORN SCREENING
Besides the fascinating science, the bigger issue raised by Ayaan's story is the question of mandatory Newborn Screening (NBS). This is conducted by means of a 'heel-prick' to draw blood from the baby within hours of birth. The blood is then screened for a limited panel of genetic conditions. The advantage is that life-threatening conditions such as metabolic diseases or PIDs can be identified and treated immediately. In addition, a baby with SCID would never receive a live vaccine as Ayaan did. NBS is now practised across all US states as well as around the world, but it is only available from one lab in SA (at NWU Potchefstroom), and most parents are not even aware of it. The financial argument for NBS is that expensive and lifelong treatment can be replaced with far cheaper interventions at birth: many of the conditions it identifies can be easily managed. Even a bone-marrow transplant at 3 months (in the case of a SCID baby) is cheaper than constant hospitalization for an endless litany of infections.


Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Cape Town to interview Ayaan's parents and paediatrician, and to film the family together.
Travel to Potchefstroom (petrol only) to interview Dr Chris Vorster at NWU's NBS lab and film the lab at work.

Press Release:


Imagine your child was born without a functioning immune system, vulnerable to the most common of infections. Ayaan Isaacs has Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, curable only by bone marrow transplant. When the search for a donor was only partially successful, his mother Shamaa Sheik turned to a clinical trial offering ground-breaking gene therapy.

Script:


UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: I sometimes don’t feel like a mother. I feel more like I’m a nurse.
VO: Ayaan was born to Shamaa Sheik and her husband Alleem Isaacs in March 2016, apparently in perfect health. But within days he was admitted to hospital with a life-threatening liver infection.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: And we never left the hospital until 4 or 5 months later.
VO: Paediatrician Dr Hedi van der Watt was part of the team battling for Ayaan’s life.
UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: We thought we were going to lose Ayaan. You get to a point where you’ve gone through the systematic approach and then you start having to throw things at a problem.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: We were told that he was not improving at all and that we needed to prepare for the worst.
UPSOUND: Alleem Isaacs: He hasn’t even enjoyed his own room, his toys. I’m never going to hear him say daddy.
VO: Eventually Ayaan began to respond to treatment. But the journey to save his life had only just begun.
Clinical pathologist Dr Sylvia van den Berg helped diagnose Ayaan with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency.
UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: Primary Immune Deficiencies are inherited flaws in the immune system. There are many PIDs described, more than 300 up to date but the most ominous of this will be SCID.
LINK: Without speedy and effective treatment, most children born with SCID will die before their first birthday.
VO: In SCID patients, the immune cells are either missing or don’t function, leaving them without an immune system. They suffer from severe, recurrent infections and failure to thrive.
UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: They cannot defend themselves against what we call less pathogenic or less virulent organisms like the common cold.
VO: SCID was made famous by David Vetter, who survived 12 years inside a sterilised plastic bubble, until his death from infection following a bone marrow transplant in 1984. Today, bone marrow transplant remains the only treatment for SCID.
UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: It is a problem in SA because we’ve got a relatively small registry that is ethnically restricted. The chances of getting a bone marrow transplant match is extremely slim.
UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: As soon as we heard that the parents and the siblings were not matched, or not suitable, we knew it was going to be a problem.
VO: Waiting for a match, Shamaa and Alleem kept Ayaan infection free at home. When a donor was found, it was only a partial match.
UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: These patients are at high risk. And if they receive a matched unrelated donor they have a larger risk to develop a disease that we call graft vs host disease. And it can be fatal.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: It was at that point I learnt about St Jude and their trial.
VO: At St Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Memphis Tennessee, Dr Ewelina Mamcarz runs a clinical trial investigating gene therapy treatment for SCID.
UPSOUND: Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: Briefly gene therapy restores a normal copy of a defective gene. So in our LVXSCID trial, our patients with X-linked SCID have a defective gene in their bone marrow stem cells. We collect this bone marrow in a procedure called harvest and then infect the cells with a virus, disabled HIV virus. It carries the normal copy of the gene into the stem cells. Then the cells are infused after a very low dose of chemotherapy at the bedside.
LINK: SCID was the first condition to be treated with gene therapy. But the cutting edge science got a bad name when complications resulted from early, high profile trials.
UPSOUND: Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: The Primary Investigator of this trial, Dr Brian Sorrentino started work on this in 1990. He came up with a vector that we believe is safer.
UPSOUND: Dr van der Watt: He was either going to die, or we could offer him this.
VO: Shamaa persuaded St Jude to accept Ayaan. In March 2017 the family left for Memphis. Within weeks, Ayaan had received his transplant but they remained in strict isolation for almost a year.
UPSOUND: Alleem Isaacs: After ten months we were there we probably went out 4 or 5 times at most.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: From four months we could already see that he was thriving better. And then from about 6 months he came off chronic medication.
LINK: Ayaan’s hospital fees cost their medical aid around R1 million in those early crisis-filled days – a cost that could have been avoided with the application of one relatively affordable test.
VO: SCID occurs in 1 in every 40 000 to 100 000 births but only five children were diagnosed in SA last year.
A working diagnosis for SCID can be made using simple tests that are widely available because they are used for HIV monitoring. Better yet is proactive newborn screening, which is standard in many countries.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: Newborn screening is screening newborn babies for rare inherited diseases, of which many are metabolic diseases that is not apparent at birth, difficult to diagnose, but treatable.
VO: Prof Chris Vorster runs the only South African laboratory with a Newborn Screening programme, at North-West University Potchefstroom.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: Currently in SA about half a percent of all newborns will receive NBS which is about 4% of all babies born in the private sector. None of the babies in the public sector will receive NBS simply because at this stage the government doesn’t reimburse the service.
VO: Globally, one in every 2000 tests detects a defect. At NWU, the screen costs just R1200, but doesn’t yet include SCID.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: A country is economically better off when they screen their newborns as opposed to when they wait for the consequences to set in and then having to deal with those consequences.
VO: In South Africa, where newborns still receive live vaccines, screening is even more vital. SCID prevented Ayaan developing immunity to the BCG vaccine, which caused the very disease it was meant to prevent: multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. But finally in January, he was cleared to come home.
LINK: The family no longer needs to live in sterilised isolation. Ayaan can go outside and make contact with the relatives who have been waiting almost two years to meet him.
UPSOUND: Alleem Isaacs: There’s a lot that he hasn’t explored outside and he only wants to be outside now.
VO: Almost two now, Ayaan is still on plenty of medication. After months of feeding via a tube, he is also learning to eat on his own.
UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: Kids with chronic disease often have an initial drawback and take a little bit longer to catch up. He will need physio, he will need a little bit of OT. But it shouldn’t impact him in later life.
VO: Gene therapy treatment will eventually go mainstream, although in South Africa, bone marrow transplant will remain the most realistic cure for SCID. St Jude will monitor Ayaan’s progress until he is 18.
UPSOUND Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: We are very excited about the preliminary results on our trial and as we can say now that we are able to restore immune system.
VO: For Shamaa and Alleem, the focus is now on enjoying normal family life, and looking forward to a new arrival.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: I’m not a carrier of the defect. And on the very rare occasion that the next baby does have it, we have a plan in place.
UPSOUND: John Webb: What are your hopes, what are your aspirations?
Alleem Isaacs: We want to do more things together that we probably took for granted in the past. I want him to play sports. I never thought about that again while he was sick. But now all those things are resurfacing again.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: We can experience things that normal families do. And we will always be grateful.

10 SEC PROMO
VO: Imagine your child was born without an immune system.
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: I sometimes don’t feel like a mother. I feel more like I’m a nurse.

15 SEC PROMO
VO: A ground-breaking clinical trial in Tennessee is offering hope for children born without a functioning immune system.
UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: He was either going to die, or we could offer him this.
UPSOUND: Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: We are very excited about the preliminary results of the trial.

15 SEC PROMO
UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: We were told that he was not improving at all and that we needed to prepare for the worst.
VO: Born without an immune system, Ayaan Isaacs is South Africa’s own ‘bubble boy’.
UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: The chances of getting a bone marrow transplant match is extremely slim.

TEASER
Imagine your child was born without an immune system. Ayaan Isaacs is the first South African child to undergo ground-breaking gene therapy for Severe Combined Immunodeficiency.

William Paul VH 0510 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 04 February 2018 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 27 February 2018 Press Release: Imagine your child was born without a functioning immune system, vulnerable to the most common of infections. Ayaan Isaacs has Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, curable only by bone marrow transplant. When the search for a donor was only partially successful, his mother Shamaa Sheik turned to a clinical trial offering ground-breaking gene therapy. Script: UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: I sometimes don’t feel like a mother. I feel more like I’m a nurse. VO: Ayaan was born to Shamaa Sheik and her husband Alleem Isaacs in March 2016, apparently in perfect health. But within days he was admitted to hospital with a life-threatening liver infection. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: And we never left the hospital until 4 or 5 months later. VO: Paediatrician Dr Hedi van der Watt was part of the team battling for Ayaan’s life. UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: We thought we were going to lose Ayaan. You get to a point where you’ve gone through the systematic approach and then you start having to throw things at a problem. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: We were told that he was not improving at all and that we needed to prepare for the worst. UPSOUND: Alleem Isaacs: He hasn’t even enjoyed his own room, his toys. I’m never going to hear him say daddy. VO: Eventually Ayaan began to respond to treatment. But the journey to save his life had only just begun. Clinical pathologist Dr Sylvia van den Berg helped diagnose Ayaan with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency. UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: Primary Immune Deficiencies are inherited flaws in the immune system. There are many PIDs described, more than 300 up to date but the most ominous of this will be SCID. LINK: Without speedy and effective treatment, most children born with SCID will die before their first birthday. VO: In SCID patients, the immune cells are either missing or don’t function, leaving them without an immune system. They suffer from severe, recurrent infections and failure to thrive. UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: They cannot defend themselves against what we call less pathogenic or less virulent organisms like the common cold. VO: SCID was made famous by David Vetter, who survived 12 years inside a sterilised plastic bubble, until his death from infection following a bone marrow transplant in 1984. Today, bone marrow transplant remains the only treatment for SCID. UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: It is a problem in SA because we’ve got a relatively small registry that is ethnically restricted. The chances of getting a bone marrow transplant match is extremely slim. UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: As soon as we heard that the parents and the siblings were not matched, or not suitable, we knew it was going to be a problem. VO: Waiting for a match, Shamaa and Alleem kept Ayaan infection free at home. When a donor was found, it was only a partial match. UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: These patients are at high risk. And if they receive a matched unrelated donor they have a larger risk to develop a disease that we call graft vs host disease. And it can be fatal. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: It was at that point I learnt about St Jude and their trial. VO: At St Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Memphis Tennessee, Dr Ewelina Mamcarz runs a clinical trial investigating gene therapy treatment for SCID. UPSOUND: Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: Briefly gene therapy restores a normal copy of a defective gene. So in our LVXSCID trial, our patients with X-linked SCID have a defective gene in their bone marrow stem cells. We collect this bone marrow in a procedure called harvest and then infect the cells with a virus, disabled HIV virus. It carries the normal copy of the gene into the stem cells. Then the cells are infused after a very low dose of chemotherapy at the bedside. LINK: SCID was the first condition to be treated with gene therapy. But the cutting edge science got a bad name when complications resulted from early, high profile trials. UPSOUND: Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: The Primary Investigator of this trial, Dr Brian Sorrentino started work on this in 1990. He came up with a vector that we believe is safer. UPSOUND: Dr van der Watt: He was either going to die, or we could offer him this. VO: Shamaa persuaded St Jude to accept Ayaan. In March 2017 the family left for Memphis. Within weeks, Ayaan had received his transplant but they remained in strict isolation for almost a year. UPSOUND: Alleem Isaacs: After ten months we were there we probably went out 4 or 5 times at most. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: From four months we could already see that he was thriving better. And then from about 6 months he came off chronic medication. LINK: Ayaan’s hospital fees cost their medical aid around R1 million in those early crisis-filled days – a cost that could have been avoided with the application of one relatively affordable test. VO: SCID occurs in 1 in every 40 000 to 100 000 births but only five children were diagnosed in SA last year. A working diagnosis for SCID can be made using simple tests that are widely available because they are used for HIV monitoring. Better yet is proactive newborn screening, which is standard in many countries. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: Newborn screening is screening newborn babies for rare inherited diseases, of which many are metabolic diseases that is not apparent at birth, difficult to diagnose, but treatable. VO: Prof Chris Vorster runs the only South African laboratory with a Newborn Screening programme, at North-West University Potchefstroom. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: Currently in SA about half a percent of all newborns will receive NBS which is about 4% of all babies born in the private sector. None of the babies in the public sector will receive NBS simply because at this stage the government doesn’t reimburse the service. VO: Globally, one in every 2000 tests detects a defect. At NWU, the screen costs just R1200, but doesn’t yet include SCID. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: A country is economically better off when they screen their newborns as opposed to when they wait for the consequences to set in and then having to deal with those consequences. VO: In South Africa, where newborns still receive live vaccines, screening is even more vital. SCID prevented Ayaan developing immunity to the BCG vaccine, which caused the very disease it was meant to prevent: multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. But finally in January, he was cleared to come home. LINK: The family no longer needs to live in sterilised isolation. Ayaan can go outside and make contact with the relatives who have been waiting almost two years to meet him. UPSOUND: Alleem Isaacs: There’s a lot that he hasn’t explored outside and he only wants to be outside now. VO: Almost two now, Ayaan is still on plenty of medication. After months of feeding via a tube, he is also learning to eat on his own. UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: Kids with chronic disease often have an initial drawback and take a little bit longer to catch up. He will need physio, he will need a little bit of OT. But it shouldn’t impact him in later life. VO: Gene therapy treatment will eventually go mainstream, although in South Africa, bone marrow transplant will remain the most realistic cure for SCID. St Jude will monitor Ayaan’s progress until he is 18. UPSOUND Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: We are very excited about the preliminary results on our trial and as we can say now that we are able to restore immune system. VO: For Shamaa and Alleem, the focus is now on enjoying normal family life, and looking forward to a new arrival. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: I’m not a carrier of the defect. And on the very rare occasion that the next baby does have it, we have a plan in place. UPSOUND: John Webb: What are your hopes, what are your aspirations? Alleem Isaacs: We want to do more things together that we probably took for granted in the past. I want him to play sports. I never thought about that again while he was sick. But now all those things are resurfacing again. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: We can experience things that normal families do. And we will always be grateful. 10 SEC PROMO VO: Imagine your child was born without an immune system. UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: I sometimes don’t feel like a mother. I feel more like I’m a nurse. 15 SEC PROMO VO: A ground-breaking clinical trial in Tennessee is offering hope for children born without a functioning immune system. UPSOUND: Dr Hedi van der Watt: He was either going to die, or we could offer him this. UPSOUND: Dr Ewelina Mamcarz: We are very excited about the preliminary results of the trial. 15 SEC PROMO UPSOUND: Shamaa Sheik: We were told that he was not improving at all and that we needed to prepare for the worst. VO: Born without an immune system, Ayaan Isaacs is South Africa’s own ‘bubble boy’. UPSOUND: Dr Sylvia van den Berg: The chances of getting a bone marrow transplant match is extremely slim. TEASER Imagine your child was born without an immune system. Ayaan Isaacs is the first South African child to undergo ground-breaking gene therapy for Severe Combined Immunodeficiency.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Groundbreaking gene therapy offers hope for a rare immune condition.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A South African first and a globally leading gene therapy clinical trial. Ayaan Ahmed Sheik, a Cape Town child has received cutting edge and apparently successful gene therapy for the rare condition, Severe Combined Immunodeficiency. This is a story that speaks not only to fascinating new technology, but to the question of whether newborn screening should be implemented in SA hospitals.
metadata.Summary: Ayaan Ahmed Sheik has spent almost all of his two years of life in hospital, battling a series of infections that threatened to end his short life. He was born with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, a rare condition that left him with no immune system at all - no defence against the hundreds of common infections that the rest of us brush off daily. Most children born with this condition die, because they are not diagnosed in time to rescue their embattled immune systems from common but - to them - life-threatening infections. SCID children who are diagnosed early enough receive a bone marrow transplant - this must be carried out within their first three months of life for maximum effect. In Ayaan's case, there was a long delay in tissue typing and searching for a donor. When a potential donor was found, it was only a partial match and his mother Shamaa considered the risk to be too high. In desperation, Shamaa reached out to St Jude Children's Hospital in Memphis Tennessee, where a clinical trial was testing ground-breaking new gene therapy for treatment of SCID. Ayaan was eventually accepted into the trial and after a long journey filled with stress and setbacks, he is now home in Cape Town, apparently able to start a normal life at last.
metadata.Further information: 1. SEVERE COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY Severe Combined Immunodeficiency is the most severe of the genetic PIDs (primary immunodeficiencies) and essentially means that you have no functioning immune system. It was first made famous by "Bubble Boy" David Vetter (b 1971), who lived until the age of 12 in a sterile bubble, before he received a bone marrow transplant that unfortunately carried an Epstein-Barr virus and killed him shortly afterwards. The story attracted enormous press attention at the time, and inspired the movies The Boy in the Plastic Bubble (1976, starring John Travolta) and Bubble Boy (2001, starring Jake Gyllenhaal), as well as a musical. Ayaan's SCID first manifested as severe and sudden illness within days of his birth. No one knew what was wrong until emergency exploratory surgery revealed multiple abscesses on his liver (an infection had entered through his umbilical cord). According to Shamaa, Ayaan is the only infant survivor of multiple liver abscesses. Following the surgery, Ayaan continued to present with severe infections and was eventually diagnosed with SCID. It’s usually an x-linked condition that is inherited from your mother, but in Ayaan’s case it is a spontaneous mutation. 2. ST JUDE CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL Initially Ayaan was too old for the St Jude clinical trial but while Shamaa was in contact with them, they amended their protocol and accepted Ayaan into their programme. St Jude is a no-fee hospital funded entirely by celebrity donors. This particular trial, which is called LVXSCID-ND, covers 12 children for 5 years at a total cost of $28 million ($2.3 million per child). The hospital funds everything for them - housing, social worker, interpreters. After the children complete initial treatment, they are followed and supported by St Jude until they reach adulthood. 3. GENE THERAPY Gene therapy has been considered for many years as a way to cure certain types of PID. But there was one very high profile clinical trial in which several of the subjects developed leukaemia following the therapy, and it got a bad name (the vector was inserted next to an important leukaemia inhibitor). The doctors at St Jude have developed a new vector which uses the HIV virus to transport the corrected genes through the body’s cells. 4. AYAAN'S TREATMENT Ayaan's treatment went well, but there were complications caused by the fact that he, like all other SA-born babies, received a mandatory live BCG vaccine days after his birth. This caused a TB-type infection on his bones. His parents both accompanied him to the States, where they had to juggle treatment and care of their son during the day, with attempting to maintain their jobs at a distance by night. His mother returned home due to ill-health and stress late in 2017, and Ayaan and his dad finally came home in January 2018. They are now adjusting to life in SA, including introducing Ayaan to family members who have never seen him. Shamaa's teenage daughter from a previous marriage was left behind while Ayaan received his treatment and the family is now reintegrating. 5. NEWBORN SCREENING Besides the fascinating science, the bigger issue raised by Ayaan's story is the question of mandatory Newborn Screening (NBS). This is conducted by means of a 'heel-prick' to draw blood from the baby within hours of birth. The blood is then screened for a limited panel of genetic conditions. The advantage is that life-threatening conditions such as metabolic diseases or PIDs can be identified and treated immediately. In addition, a baby with SCID would never receive a live vaccine as Ayaan did. NBS is now practised across all US states as well as around the world, but it is only available from one lab in SA (at NWU Potchefstroom), and most parents are not even aware of it. The financial argument for NBS is that expensive and lifelong treatment can be replaced with far cheaper interventions at birth: many of the conditions it identifies can be easily managed. Even a bone-marrow transplant at 3 months (in the case of a SCID baby) is cheaper than constant hospitalization for an endless litany of infections.
